transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-21
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Lucas Patel (Redwood SE), Dan Ruiz (NimblePay CTO), Sofia Ortiz (NimblePay ML Eng), Marcus Lee (NimblePay Platform)
Recording ID: ff-20261221-93ab

Summary:
Quick hosted API intro focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming behavior, generation params (temperature/top_p/max_tokens), and retry/backoff strategies. Customer wanted reassurance on latency, cost tradeoffs, and security for PCI adjacent flows. Agreed next steps: share benchmark sheet, run customer-specific microbench, and schedule pilot kickoff in early January.

Topics:
- Hosted API streaming semantics and event model
- Best-practice parameters for short multi-turn chat vs long responses
- Retry patterns, idempotency considerations, and handling partial streams
- Console/Optimize pointers for batching and token-cost control
- Security/QoS: encryption, retention, SOC2 questions raised

Action items (captured live):
- Maya: pricing + latency sheet (send by 1/4)
- Lucas: run small bench on customer's sample payloads (share by 1/6)
- Dan: provide sample traffic profile and request logs (by 12/28)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Maya, I'm the AE on the account, and Lucas from our SRE/SE team is here to run through the hosted API behaviors and answer deep technical questions.
[00:10] Dan Ruiz: Cool, thanks. We just have a few folks — me, Sofia from ML, and Marcus for infra. We're trying to understand, like, what happens when we stream long receipts back to users, and how retries won't double-bill us or create duplicate charges.
[00:25] Lucas Patel: Yeah I hear you. We usually, um, we recommend a streaming-first approach for interactive UIs — you get tokens as they generate — and we have a couple of levers: chunk sizes, early stop heuristics, and prefix caching.
[00:40] Sofia Ortiz: Quick question — when you say prefix caching, do you mean the KV-cache at the runtime level or something at the routing layer?
[00:48] Lucas Patel: Good callout. At runtime we keep a per-session KV cache of keys for autoregressive decoding — that's the one that speeds up repeated context patterns. There's also a higher-level prefix cache we can enable for repeated prompts, which reduces token compute. The naming in our docs is a bit messy — sometimes shows up as "KV cache" or "prefix cache" — apologies, we had an internal rename last quarter.
[01:10] Marcus Lee: And does that work for multi-region? Our users are global and we can't afford extra round trips for cache misses.
[01:18] Lucas Patel: The cache is local to the serving pool; smart routing will pin requests by region where possible. If you enable cross-region replicas, the cache warmup is replicated asynchronously but we still recommend colocating traffic for the lowest p99 latency.
[01:30] Dan Ruiz: Speaking of p99, our SLO is 400ms p95 for short messages. Is that reasonable on hosted?
[01:38] Maya Chen: We see p95 numbers under 200–300ms for small chat payloads on our fast models in most regions, but it depends on batch behavior and token length. For consistent p95 you'll want to reduce batching windows or pick a lower-latency model.
[01:52] Marcus Lee: So tradeoff is cost vs latency — smaller batch = higher cost?
[01:55] Lucas Patel: Exactly. Batching improves throughput but adds a small queuing delay. Our Console and Optimize tool will give recommendations per workload — like recommended max-batch and target latency.
[02:08] Sofia Ortiz: Can we see an example of a streaming response and how we'd resume if a connection drops mid-stream?
[02:15] Lucas Patel: Yeah let me sketch the flow. (pause) In a typical stream, you open a websocket or SSE, we send incremental deltas with token fragments. If the connection resets, the client should re-issue the generation request with the same idempotency key and the same conversation context. On the server side we attempt to resume from the last committed token if the KV cache is warm — otherwise you'll get a truncated restart.
[02:40] Dan Ruiz: Wait how do idempotency keys work with streaming? If we re-try, will we get duplicates?
[02:46] Lucas Patel: Good question. Our hosted API supports idempotency tokens at the request level — if a request with the same key arrives within the dedupe window, we will return the original response when possible; for streaming we send a final completion event that's correlated. There's edge cases if the original run was partial and not persisted — that's where you may see a restart. We recommend client-side logic to dedupe by tracking the final completion event and sequence offsets.
[03:10] Sofia Ortiz: Do you log partial outputs? For compliance we'd need to know what was generated and when.
[03:15] Maya Chen: By default, generated content is logged for debugging but can be disabled for privacy. For enterprise/private deployments we have retention controls and can integrate with KMS so logs are encrypted at rest. We'll share the security whitepaper after this call.
[03:30] Marcus Lee: You mentioned dedupe window — how long is it?
[03:33] Lucas Patel: The default dedupe window is 5 minutes for hosted API, configurable for enterprise customers. If you need longer retention of idempotency, we can extend it in Dedicated or Private deployments.
[03:42] Dan Ruiz: Another practical: how should we tune temperature and top_p for short transactional messages? We want deterministic confirmations vs helpful expansions.
[03:52] Lucas Patel: For deterministic transactional outputs we recommend low temperature, near-zero (0–0.2), and top_p around 0.6–0.9 depending on the model. Lower max_tokens and a strict stop sequence helps ensure you don't get verbose run-ons. We also advise using system prompts that constrain the output shape.
[04:10] Sofia Ortiz: Are there built-in tools to enforce output length? We have downstream parsers that fail on extra words.
[04:16] Maya Chen: Two approaches: token limit (max_tokens) and stop sequences — also you can use the structured output features to request JSON with a schema; the runtime will still be probabilistic but we provide higher-level reranking/validate hooks in Optimize to reduce schema breaks.
[04:34] Dan Ruiz: What about retries when calls fail due to transient infra errors? If we just naively retry, could we charge double?
[04:41] Lucas Patel: Charges are based on completed tokens. If a request fails before completion, typically nothing is billed for partial work — though there are rare edge cases. We have explicit semantics: if the server sends an error and no final completion, we treat it as failed and don't bill for the incomplete chunks. But if a chunk was fully processed, that might be billed. We'll give you the exact billing doc.
[05:05] Marcus Lee: Could you outline a recommended client backoff? Exponential? Jitter?
[05:10] Lucas Patel: Use exponential backoff with jitter. Example: initial retry after 250ms, multiply by 2, cap at 8s, randomize +-20% jitter. For streaming, prefer reconnect-and-resume where the idempotency key helps. For long-running generations use longer timeouts on the client to avoid premature retry.
[05:30] Sofia Ortiz: Do you support a resumable token offset so we can request generation starting from token 120 or something?
[05:36] Lucas Patel: We don't currently expose token-offset resume APIs to customers, mainly because tokenization can differ across model families. We do provide sequence-correlation IDs and the runtime will attempt to resume when it can. For strict resumability we typically recommend persisting partial outputs on the client and replaying context on retry.
[05:55] Dan Ruiz: For our proof-of-concept, we'll be sending 2–3k short receipts per minute — most under 80 tokens. Can you give a ballpark on cost and latency?
[06:05] Maya Chen: Ballpark depends on the model family. For small gen models you might see $0.0007–0.001 per 1k tokens for hosted, but let's not quote a hard number here — I'll send the pricing sheet. Latency: with small tokens and a tuned batch you can hit <200ms p95 in US regions.
[06:22] Marcus Lee: Whoops that's a big range. We'll need the benchmarking with our payloads.
[06:26] Maya Chen: Yep, Lucas will run a microbench. Can you share sample payloads and target qps?
[06:32] Dan Ruiz: I'll put those in a folder — mostly templates and 80-token examples — can that be by Tuesday?
[06:36] Maya Chen: That works, thanks.
[06:39] --- (transcript jumps, small gap in auto-transcription) ---
[07:05] Lucas Patel: I'll show a quick demo — let's pretend we have a simple SSE stream. (describes code) On connect, you get "delta" events with pieces, then a "done" event. If you miss a 'delta' you can replay the final by requesting the completed idempotent result.
[07:30] Sofia Ortiz: Sounds good — does the console show the same deltas for debugging?
[07:34] Lucas Patel: Yes, Console -> Live Traces will show streamed events; you can replay individual requests from the console for debugging. It also surfaces cost per request and token breakdowns.
[07:45] Dan Ruiz: Any gotchas around chunk sizes — we saw the model occasionally cut sentences mid-word in another provider.
[07:52] Lucas Patel: Chunking is on our side; fragmentation usually happens at token boundaries but occasionally OCR/tokenizer mismatches can make it look like mid-word. If that's frequent we'd look at your tokenizer and pre-tokenize locally to align.
[08:05] Marcus Lee: Security — SOC2, SSO, KMS. We need to know baseline for compliance review.
[08:11] Maya Chen: We are SOC 2 Type II certified and have SSO via SAML/OIDC; for key management we support customer-managed keys via KMS integrations in Private deployments. For hosted, we encrypt at rest and in transit; the security pack has specifics.
[08:25] Dan Ruiz: Is VPC peering possible for hosted?
[08:27] Maya Chen: For hosted we don't do direct VPC peering. For Private deployment (VPC or on-prem) yes. For Dedicated reserved capacity we can negotiate more isolated network setups.
[08:38] Sofia Ortiz: If we need to keep generated content out of logs for PCI, is that a toggle?
[08:42] Maya Chen: Yes, we can disable logging of generated content and only keep metadata (latency/size/error codes). For audit needs we can offer encrypted audit logs integrated with your KMS in Private mode.
[08:56] Dan Ruiz: There's a bit of concern from finance about competitor lock-in. If we decide to move later, how easy is it to export model artifacts or logs?
[09:05] Lucas Patel: For hosted models we don't ship model weights, obviously. But you can export the conversation logs and usage metrics. For deterministic migrations people often run pilot runs against open models locally for parity checks. The Console's export functionality lets you get token-level traces and prompt/response pairs.
[09:22] Marcus Lee: Could you walk through a short error scenario? Like 500 from model infra mid-stream and what client sees.
[09:28] Lucas Patel: If the infra throws a 5xx mid-stream, the stream typically closes with an error event. The client should treat that as incomplete and either retry with the same idempotency key or surface to the user. If you want graceful degradation, route fallback policy can call a smaller cheaper model to produce a short-confirmation response.
[09:50] Sofia Ortiz: How are fallbacks configured? Auto or manual?
[09:53] Maya Chen: You can set routing policies in Console: prefer low-latency region, then cost-tier fallback sequences to cheaper models, and set automatic fallback thresholds (error rate or latency). It's policy-driven.
[10:05] Dan Ruiz: Okay, high-level next steps — send us examples of recommended param sets for: transactional receipts (short), conversational help (longer), and batch offline summarization.
[10:15] Maya Chen: We'll include that in the benchmark/pricing sheet.
[10:18] Marcus Lee: Also please include guidance on batch sizes for 2–3k qps — we need conservative starting configs.
[10:23] Lucas Patel: Yep we'll include recommended max batch, concurrency limits, and a suggested autoscale policy.
[10:28] --- (customer asks about outages) ---
[10:40] Dan Ruiz: In worst-case outage, how quickly can Redwood failover to a cheaper model or another region?
[10:47] Lucas Patel: Automated region failover can be configured — typically within a minute depending on DNS TTLs and routing warmup. Model fallback to a lighter variant is near-instant if the variant is already loaded in the pool; otherwise there's a small cold-start. We recommend warm standby for critical flows.
[11:05] Sofia Ortiz: Any recommended metrics we should monitor?
[11:08] Maya Chen: Track p95/p99 latency, token cost per request, error rates (5xx/4xx), and drop rate for early-stops. Console has dashboards and alerting hooks.
[11:18] Dan Ruiz: For the pilot, can we get a simple SLA for latency/uptime?
[11:23] Maya Chen: For pilot we'll provide target latency guidance; formal SLA is part of Dedicated agreements. Hosted has best-effort but we can discuss an interim commitment for the pilot.
[11:33] Marcus Lee: Okay that's reasonable.
[11:35] --- (wrap up, last 5 minutes) ---
[12:05] Maya Chen: Quick recap: Lucas will run bench with your samples; Dan will drop sample payloads and qps; we'll send pricing/latency sheet and security pack; schedule pilot kickoff for week of Jan 4. Anything else?
[12:18] Dan Ruiz: Could you also include suggested client SDK patterns for reconnect and dedupe?
[12:22] Lucas Patel: Yes — we'll attach a minimal library and reconnect sample.
[12:25] Sofia Ortiz: And can we get a short doc on how structured output with schema validation integrates with Optimize?
[12:30] Maya Chen: We'll include a short doc and sample prompts — Lucas will point to the Optimize recommendations.
[12:35] Marcus Lee: Alright that's it from us.
[12:37] Maya Chen: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the items.

End of transcript.
